pageTitle: Sensory ability in the narwhal tooth organ system
quote: The erupted tusk of the narwhal exhibits sensory ability. The hypothesized sensory pathway begins with ocean water entering through cementum channels to a network of patent dentinal tubules ... Final confirmation of sensory ability is demonstrated by significant changes in heart rate when alternating solutions of high-salt and fresh water are exposed to the external tusk surface.
correctedFact: A narwhal's spiral tusk is actually a tooth, and it can sense the water around it. Seawater seeps through tiny channels in the tusk toward nerves inside, and when scientists washed tusks with alternating salty and fresh water, the narwhals' heart rates changed significantly.
note: Original paper (Nweeia et al.), PubMed abstract. Tusk length and temperature sensing are not in it. Press coverage of the same team gives about 9 feet, not 10.

pageTitle: Koala | San Diego Zoo Animals & Plants
quote: They need to sleep a lot to give them time to digest their food. ... They don't get many calories from their diet, but they conserve energy by moving occasionally and by sleeping as much as 20 hours each day. ... To conserve energy, koalas sleep 18 to 22 hours a day.

pageTitle: Female behaviour drives expression and evolution of gustatory receptors in butterflies
quote: We also show that the legs of adult female butterflies, which are used by females when selecting a host plant on which to lay their eggs, express more gustatory (taste) receptor genes than those of male butterflies. ... To ascertain host-plant identity, female butterflies drum with their legs on the surface of leaves before laying eggs. This behaviour presumably allows the female to taste oviposition stimulants.
note: Original paper (Briscoe et al.). The egg-laying taste check is done by females; the paper also notes nymphalid legs carry taste sensilla.

pageTitle: From the field: In the sea, comets become stars.
quote: the most striking examples come from the sea stars in the genus Linckia. These sea stars can drop off an arm and from it, it will regrow a complete an[imal] ... If many species of sea stars can regrow a missing arm, only a few can, like Linckia multifora, regrow a full animal from just an arm.
unsupported: A single starfish arm can regenerate an entire new body (true only of a few species, such as Linckia); Some species can even split in half and grow into two complete starfish
correctedFact: Many sea stars can regrow a lost arm, but only a few, such as the comet star Linckia multifora, can regrow a whole animal from a single arm. The dropped arm sprouts four tiny new arms, giving it a comet shape until it grows back into a full star.
note: Invertebrate Zoology blog of the Florida Museum. Splitting in half is mentioned only for flatworms on this page.

pageTitle: Hum's the word - Charlotte Urban Institute
quote: The typical speed of their wing beats ranges from 12 to 80 times per second, with an average of around 50 per second. They can also hover in mid-air by rapidly flapping their wings ... For perspective, during intense flight their heart rate can get as high as 1,260 beats per minute.
note: University outreach article, not a research page. It also claims up to 200 wingbeats per second while hovering, which conflicts with 'up to 80'; the card's numbers match its typical range. The 1,260 figure is a peak in flight for one species in the literature.

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
pageTitle: Alpaca | Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
quote: Alpacas rarely spit at people unless frightened or abused, but will use this form of communication with each other to register a complaint. ... Alpacas are social herd animals, and their only defense is flight.
unsupported: competing for food; It's their main defense mechanism (the source says their only defense is flight); can travel up to 10 feet
correctedFact: Alpacas rarely spit at people unless they are frightened or mistreated. Spitting is mostly something they do to each other: it is how one alpaca registers a complaint with another. When real danger shows up, an alpaca's only defense is to run.
note: Purdue Extension breed ID PDF (spit when threatened or irritated) failed to load. The source contradicts 'main defense mechanism'.

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
pageTitle: Smithsonian Scientists Aid in Decoding a Mammalian Mystery: The Genetics of the Pangolin
quote: They are the only mammals that are entirely covered in scales and can curl into a ball when frightened.
note: 'Living pinecones' is the card's own simile.

pageTitle: The blob blog | Te Papa's Blog
quote: Their comedic melting in air isn't because of the loss of pressure, although the cold and pressure at depth likely keeps the gel firmer, but because the support given by water has been removed. Gravity then takes over ... The lips sag into a frown, a fold of skin flops forward forming a drooping nose, and an icon is born. ... Photographed in their proper environment, blobfish are more like tadpoles on steroids, sometimes with striking patterns and frills.
unsupported: the pressure keeps it looking like a normal fish (curators say the water's support, not pressure, is the main reason); with a big nose (the drooping nose forms only out of water)
correctedFact: The blobfish only looks like a sad blob out of water. Its body is mostly a gel about as dense as seawater, and once the water's support is gone, gravity makes it sag into a frown and droopy nose. Seen in the deep sea, blobfish look more like giant tadpoles.
note: Blog by Te Papa fish curators involved in the expedition behind the famous photo. Britannica credits decompression instead; the curators explicitly reject pressure as the main cause.

publisher: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance Library
pageTitle: Physical Characteristics - Giraffes (Giraffa spp.) Fact Sheet
quote: An early study (Goetz 1955) reported a very large (11.25 kg) heart for giraffes, but this may have been an error in measurement. A comprehensive study of the giraffe cardiovascular system (Mitchell and Skinner 2009) showed heart size relative to body mass to be comparable to that of other mammals. ... As a giraffe grows, the left ventricular and interventricular walls become much thicker than in other mammals, enabling the heart to contract much more strongly. ... Systemic blood pressure at the heart with the neck held 55° to the vertical is calculated to be 208 mm Hg, nearly twice the predicted value for other species of similar size.
unsupported: giraffe blood pressure runs roughly twice that of humans (source compares with mammals of similar size); 6-foot neck
correctedFact: A 1955 study said a giraffe's heart weighed about 11 kg (25 pounds), but that was probably a measuring error. A 2009 study found the heart is normal-sized for the giraffe's body. What sets it apart is extra-thick walls that pump hard enough to push blood pressure to nearly twice that of similar-sized mammals.
extraPoints: Giraffe blood pressure is about twice normal, driven by a thick-walled heart
note: SDZWA Library fact sheet, citing Goetz 1955 and Mitchell and Skinner 2009 (Comp Biochem Physiol A). The heart-weight myth and the blood-pressure point are two separate claims.

publisher: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance Library
pageTitle: Physical Characteristics - Polar Bear (Ursus maritimus) Fact Sheet
quote: Distinctive white hair. Translucent; no pigments ... Black nose, skin, and claws
unsupported: (to absorb heat); Their fur only appears white because it reflects visible light, like snow
correctedFact: Under all that white fur, a polar bear has black skin, and so are its nose and claws. The fur itself has no pigment at all: each hair is translucent. The coat can even look yellowish in summer, stained by sunlight and oils from the seals the bear eats.
note: First page tried (SDZWA animal page) confirms clear, hollow hairs but not black skin. Library fact sheet used instead. Heat absorption and the light-reflection explanation are not on either page.

pageTitle: What makes each of us unique? The nine-banded armadillo as a model to study individuality
quote: Armadillos are part of the genus Dasypus, the only group of mammals that presents mandatory polyembryony, a unique reproductive strategy that occurs when a fertilized egg always splits into multiples, naturally originating genetically identical individuals ... The fact that armadillos always give birth to quadruplets that share the same embryonic environment within one placenta ...
note: Peer-reviewed review. Other sources note occasional litters other than four, but this source says 'always'.

pageTitle: Mitochondria and the Frozen Frog
quote: When frozen, wood frogs have no detectable vital signs: no heartbeat, breathing, blood circulation, muscle movement, or detectable brain activity. They survive for weeks/months with up to 65–70% of total body water converted into extracellular ice ... damage due to increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation can be high during thawing when breathing and heartbeat resume
note: Review by Storey, Wu and Storey (Carleton University), the lab that pioneered wood frog freeze tolerance work. Source gives 65 to 70%.

pageTitle: Caribbean sharp-nose-puffer - Lamar University
quote: Puffer fish are so named because of their ability to inflate their bodies as a defense against predators. Puffers inflate their bodies by filling it with air or water. This causes them to appear larger and it also makes them harder for predators to swallow. Puffer fish also have poisonous flesh filled with tetrodotoxin that keeps them from being readily preyed upon.
unsupported: to three times their normal size; 1,200 times more deadly than cyanide
correctedFact: Pufferfish defend themselves by gulping water or air and inflating their bodies. Puffing up makes them look bigger and much harder for a predator to swallow. As a second line of defense, their flesh is loaded with tetrodotoxin, a poison that keeps most predators from eating them.
extraPoints: Pufferfish carry a toxin far deadlier than cyanide
note: Weak source: a student-written page on a university biology site. Britannica and Texas A&M Galveston pages would not load. The Hong Kong Centre for Food Safety says tetrodotoxin is 'over 1,000 times more toxic to humans than cyanide according to some authorities' but does not cover inflation.

pageTitle: Feeding the Hospitalized Snake - LafeberVet
quote: Defining anorexia in snakes can be tricky. Fasting may be expected in some species during certain times of the year. For instance many gravid females and actively breeding males eat less or go off feed entirely. ... Prolonged or multiple fasts in less than ideal conditions can be debilitating ... Regular weighing is therefore recommended for fasting reptiles.
unsupported: Ball pythons specifically; can go months without eating
correctedFact: Many snakes eat less or stop eating while they breed. Veterinarians note that gravid females and actively breeding males often go off their food entirely, so a breeding-season fast can be expected and is not automatically a sign of illness. Weighing the snake regularly shows whether a fast is becoming a problem.
note: Veterinarian-written clinical reference (Christal Pollock, DVM). It covers snakes in general, not ball pythons. A second search for a ball python specific source found only a thesis and a 1987 paper noting males ate sporadically.

pageTitle: Central Bearded Dragon - The Australian Museum
quote: Submission is signalled by waving the forearm, which generally defuses the confrontation ... Arm waving is used by both sexes; males use waving to show submission to a dominant male, females will arm wave to show responsiveness to a male, combined with a slow head bob.
unsupported: and a polite greeting in dragon language
correctedFact: Bearded dragons wave a front leg to say 'I give up.' A male waves to show submission to a dominant male, which usually defuses the standoff before it becomes a fight. Females wave too, but for them it signals interest in a male, usually paired with a slow head bob.
note: Source frames the wave as submission or female receptiveness, not a greeting.

pageTitle: Cryptosporidium varanii Infection in Captive Leopard Gecko (Eublepharis macularius) and Its Association with Wasting Syndrome in Thailand
quote: two = thin (Minimal fat deposits in the body, the tail is straight and thin, the vertebral column is visible, but not prominent); three = average (Tail is slightly plump ...); Four = fat (Fat deposits have noticeably thickened the tail ...) ... This syndrome is characterized by anorexia, chronic weight loss, extreme emaciation (especially at the tail) ... Stress from poor management such as overcrowding, lack of heat, dehydration, irregular photoperiod, or inadequate diet may induce this syndrome
note: Peer-reviewed paper using a body condition score built on tail fat. LafeberVet's leopard gecko sheet also says the healthy gecko 'deposits significant fat stores in its tail base'.

pageTitle: Crested Gecko | Habitat, Diet & Comeback | Connecticut's Beardsley Zoo
quote: Crested Geckos live in the canopies of rainforests on the New Caledonia Islands. ... For many years, they were believed to be extinct before being rediscovered in 1994.
unsupported: They're now one of the most popular gecko species in the hobby
correctedFact: Crested geckos live in the rainforest canopy of New Caledonia, and for many years scientists believed they were extinct. Then in 1994 the species was rediscovered, one of the most surprising comebacks in the reptile world. Today it is listed as Vulnerable.
extraPoints: Crested geckos are now among the most popular pet geckos
note: AZA-accredited zoo page; cites Smithsonian National Zoo and IUCN. Popularity in the pet trade is not on the page.

pageTitle: Selection for social signalling drives the evolution of chameleon colour change
quote: Overall, our results suggest that the evolution of the ability to exhibit striking changes in colour evolved as a strategy to facilitate social signalling and not, as popularly believed, camouflage. ... all dwarf chameleons show capacity for substantial change in brightness in a variety of contexts including thermoregulation, female aggressive rejection displays, and camouflage, whereas marked chromatic change is most prevalent in social contexts.
unsupported: Color changes signal stress, excitement, readiness to mate (the paper shows dominance, submission and female rejection displays)
correctedFact: Chameleons didn't evolve their dramatic color changes mainly for camouflage. A study of dwarf chameleons found the bright color shifts evolved for social signaling, like flashing dominant or submissive colors at rivals. Smaller changes in brightness also help with temperature control and camouflage.
note: Original paper (Stuart-Fox and Moussalli), on southern African dwarf chameleons.

pageTitle: Eye Structure and Function in Dogs - Dog Owners - Merck Veterinary Manual
quote: The eyes of a dog are protected not only by the same types of eyelids that people have, but also by the nictitating membrane, which is sometimes called the third eyelid. This additional eyelid is a whitish pink color, and it is found under the lower eyelids on the inside corner of the eye (near the nose). The third eyelid extends across the eye when needed to protect the eyeball from scratches (for example, while traveling through brush) or in response to inflammation.
unsupported: and moisten the eye; You can sometimes spot it when a dog is sleepy
correctedFact: Dogs have three eyelids. Besides the upper and lower lids, a whitish pink third eyelid called the nictitating membrane sits in the inner corner of each eye. It sweeps across the eye when needed, protecting it from scratches, such as when a dog pushes through brush.

pageTitle: Study on the Viability of Canine Nose Pattern as a Unique Biometric Marker
quote: It was found that the canine nose pattern remains invariant regardless of when the image is taken; and that the canine nose pattern is indeed unique to each dog. ... the most well-known example is that of the Canadian Kennel Club accepting canine nose prints as proof of identity since 1938.
unsupported: Some kennel clubs have started using nose prints (the documented example, the Canadian Kennel Club, has accepted them since 1938)
correctedFact: The pattern of bumps and grooves on a dog's nose is unique to that dog and stays the same over time, much like a human fingerprint. As far back as 1938, the Canadian Kennel Club accepted inked nose prints as proof of a dog's identity.
note: Peer-reviewed study of 60 dogs (70 in the enlarged set). 'Started' implies a recent trend; the kennel club use dates to 1938.

publisher: Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine
pageTitle: Sleeping Disorders in Animals | Pet Talk
quote: However, we will never really know if pets dream because we cannot talk to them. However, we do know that dogs have the REM sleep phase and this is the dream activity period in people. Dogs do have leg movements, facial twitching, vocalizations, and tail movements. Therefore, it might be likely they are having a dream.
unsupported: Dogs dream just like humans do (stated as fact; the source says it is likely but unknowable); remarkably similar to ours; as they relive their day
correctedFact: Dogs probably dream. They have REM sleep, the stage when people do most of their dreaming, and during it they twitch their legs and faces, wag their tails and make little noises. Since dogs can't tell us, vets say it is likely they are dreaming but we can't know for sure.
note: Quote from Dr. M.A. Crist, Texas A&M veterinary faculty.

pageTitle: Congenital Deafness and Its Recognition | Deafness in Dogs & Cats
quote: Sensory function in neonatal dogs and cats is primarily tactile, olfactory and gustatory. The visual and auditory senses, although partially functional at birth, exhibit significant postnatal development: in the dog, the eyes do not open until a puppy is 8 to 10 days of age, the ear canals do not open until it is 12 to 13 days of age
unsupported: completely blind and deaf (source says partially functional); rely entirely on smell and touch (source adds taste and says 'primarily'); eyes open around 2 weeks (source gives 8 to 10 days)
correctedFact: Newborn puppies get around mostly by touch, smell and taste. Their sight and hearing work only a little at birth because their eyes and ear canals are still sealed shut. A puppy's eyes open at about 8 to 10 days old, and its ear canals open at about 12 to 13 days.
note: Text of George Strain's review (originally Veterinary Clinics of North America), hosted by LSU.

pageTitle: Puppy Exercise and Mental Stimulation
quote: Most puppies benefit from daily enrichment activities such as training, puzzle toys, scent games, and social experiences. Mental exercise can be just as tiring as physical activity for many dogs. ... Cognitive challenges will also help curtail destructive behaviors by keeping your puppy entertained. Not to mention, mental exercise can be just as exhausting as the physical kind.
note: Weakest kind of support: expert advice, not a study. The source hedges ('can be', 'for many dogs'). An Ohio State behavioral medicine handout supports enrichment but not the 'as tiring' comparison; no controlled study found.

pageTitle: Feline vocal communication
quote: More than that, it seems that the house cat actually specialized their meow to communicate with humans and not with conspecifics. ... Instead of creating new vocalization types, it is more probable that the cat has modified the function of some of its vocalizations to communicate adequately with humans. ... the literature corroborates a large variation intra- and inter-individual in the vocal production.
unsupported: only ... not at other cats (source says 'it seems', and kittens call to mothers); They invented the meow (source says cats more probably modified existing calls); each cat develops its own unique vocabulary
correctedFact: Adult house cats seem to save their meows mostly for people rather than other cats. Researchers think cats didn't invent a new sound for us: they repurposed an existing call to get our attention. Feral cats barely meow around a caretaker at first, but meow more after weeks of regular contact.
extraPoints: Each cat develops its own unique vocabulary with its owner
note: Peer-reviewed review. 'Invented' is contradicted by the source.

publisher: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America (2001)
pageTitle: The felid purr: A healing mechanism?
quote: Every felid in the study generated strong frequencies between 25 and 150 Hz. Purr frequencies correspond to vibrational/electrical frequencies used in treatment for bone growth/fractures, pain, edema, muscle growth/strain, joint flexibility, dyspnea, and wounds. Domestic cats, servals, ocelots, and pumas produce fundamental, dominant, or strong frequencies at exactly 25 Hz and 50 Hz, the two low frequencies that best promote bone growth/fracture healing
unsupported: a frequency known to promote bone healing (the abstract proposes this as a hypothesis); reduce stress; for both the cat and the human nearby
correctedFact: Every cat species in one acoustic study, from house cats to cheetahs, purred at strong frequencies between 25 and 150 Hz. Those happen to match the vibration frequencies used in therapy for healing bones, which has led one researcher to suggest purring may help cats heal themselves.
note: Conference abstract (von Muggenthaler, Fauna Communications Research Institute), not a full paper. The healing link is a hypothesis; nothing in it concerns humans or stress.
